pattern.label: Circulation pattern
pattern.help: A large-scale arrangement of pressure and wind. It does not fix the weather on its own.

air-mass.label: Air mass / airflow
air-mass.help: A body of air with a source region and track that set its temperature, moisture and stability.

scenario.label: Weather scenario
scenario.help: A recognisable combination of conditions and the weather it tends to produce.

hazard.label: Hazard
hazard.help: A condition that can cause harm or disruption.

process.label: Meteorological process
process.help: A physical mechanism that operates inside many scenarios.

phenomenon.label: Observable phenomenon
phenomenon.help: Something you can see or measure; often harmless, sometimes a sign of a process.

C.label: Seasonally common
C.def: A well-established, recurrent type of weather for this month or season. Most years will see it somewhere in the UK.

P.label: Plausible
P.def: Meteorologically possible and not unusual to see in some years, but with no implication that it is expected this month.

U.label: Uncommon
U.def: Happens less regularly, or needs a less typical combination of ingredients. Many years pass without it in this month.

R.label: Rare or exceptional
R.def: Supported by the observational record as a relatively unusual occurrence in this month, usually because the setup it needs is unusual.

-.label: Outside its season
-.def: Not a recognised feature of this month in the UK record. This is NOT a claim that it is impossible — only that it is not documented as part of this month's weather.

frequencyNotes: These labels describe climatology — how often a type of weather has historically turned up in a month — not the chance of it happening in any particular forecast.
They are qualitative. Where a reliable quantitative figure exists it is shown separately, with its source, area and reference period.
A label applies to the UK as a whole unless the regional view says otherwise; a "common" scenario can still be rare in some regions.
No recurrence periods are invented. Where a source gives one, it is quoted with that source.

low.label: Low
low.def: Usually little disruption; worth knowing about.

moderate.label: Moderate
moderate.def: Can cause local disruption or difficult conditions.

high.label: High
high.def: Can cause significant disruption, damage or danger to life in the worst-affected areas.

very-high.label: Very high
very-high.def: Capable of widespread damage, major disruption and loss of life.

regions.name: South East England
regions.factors: The warmest and driest part of the UK in summer and the most continental in character: furthest from the Atlantic, closest to the near continent. Hot plumes and the highest temperatures usually reach here first. Chalk downland and the long south coast give sea-breeze contrasts; the Weald and Thames valley collect cold air on clear nights.

regions.name: London
regions.factors: A large urban heat island: nights stay warmer than the surrounding countryside, which matters most in heatwaves. Extensive hard surfaces make surface-water flooding from intense rain a particular risk. The tidal Thames links the city to North Sea surge events, managed by the Thames Barrier.

regions.name: East of England
regions.factors: Low-lying, relatively dry and exposed to the North Sea. Among the most frequently thundery parts of the UK in summer, and well placed for North Sea snow showers in cold easterlies. Long, low coastlines and the fens make coastal and tidal flooding an important hazard; the region is also prone to agricultural drought.

regions.name: South West England
regions.factors: The most Atlantic-facing part of England: mild winters, frequent wind and rain, and the first landfall for many storms and ex-tropical systems. Dartmoor, Exmoor and Bodmin Moor wring extra rain from moist air, and steep, short river catchments (Boscastle, Lynmouth) can respond violently to intense rain.

regions.name: East Midlands
regions.factors: Inland and fairly continental for England: warm summers and among the most thundery areas of the country. The Peak District rises to over 600 m in the north-west. The Trent and its tributaries collect water from a large catchment.

regions.name: West Midlands
regions.factors: Inland, sheltered somewhat by Wales from the Atlantic. The Severn, Wye, Teme and Avon drain large areas of Wales and the Marches, so the region often floods from rain that fell further west. Cold air pools in valleys on clear winter nights.

regions.name: Yorkshire and the Humber
regions.factors: From the Pennines and Dales in the west to the North Sea coast in the east. Pennine rain and snow, sheltered lowlands in the Vale of York, North Sea haar and snow showers on the coast, and large river systems (Ouse, Aire, Don) draining to the Humber.

regions.name: North West England
regions.factors: Faces the prevailing south-westerlies off the Irish Sea. The Lake District fells hold several UK rainfall records, and orographic rain over Cumbria and the Pennines drives major river floods (Carlisle 2005, Cumbria 2009 and 2015). Irish Sea snow showers can reach the Cheshire Gap in northerly flows.

regions.name: North East England
regions.factors: Sheltered from the west by the Pennines, so drier than the north-west, but exposed to the North Sea. Easterly and north-easterly winds bring snow, haar and cold; north-westerly storms gust strongly down the Pennine slopes and across Northumberland.

regions.name: Wales
regions.factors: Mountainous and Atlantic-facing. Snowdonia, the Cambrian Mountains and the Brecon Beacons take very high rainfall, feeding rivers that flood both Wales and the English Marches. Exposed western headlands record some of the UK's highest gusts; valleys hold cold air and fog.

regions.name: Southern Scotland
regions.factors: Dumfries and Galloway, the Borders, Ayrshire and South Lanarkshire. The Southern Uplands catch Atlantic rain in the west and shelter the Borders to the east, where some of Scotland's warmest summer temperatures have been recorded. Exposed to storms tracking across northern England.

regions.name: Central Scotland
regions.factors: The Central Belt (Glasgow to Edinburgh) plus Fife, Perthshire and Tayside. A west–east contrast: wetter and windier around the Clyde, drier towards the Forth and Tay. Strong winds funnel through the Central Belt in some storms; easterly flows bring snow and haar to Fife and the Lothians.

regions.name: Northern Scotland and the Highlands
regions.factors: The Highlands, Grampians, Moray, Aberdeenshire and Argyll. The UK's highest mountains and coldest glens (Braemar, Altnaharra), the most lying snow, and a strong west–east contrast: very wet western mountains, a drier east with föhn warmth in some westerly and southerly flows.

regions.name: The Scottish Islands
regions.factors: The Western Isles, Orkney and Shetland. The most exposed part of the UK: closest to Atlantic storm tracks, with frequent gales and very few frosts, cool summers, and long daylight in midsummer. Sea temperatures dominate the climate.

regions.name: Northern Ireland
regions.factors: Maritime and mild, with the Atlantic to the west and the Irish Sea to the east. The Mournes and Sperrins add orographic rain; Lough Neagh and the inland lowlands can be notably warmer in summer and colder on clear winter nights than the coasts.

months.title: January — winter weather and Atlantic storms
months.tagline: Mild Atlantic gales or bitter continental cold — the month can go either way.
months.intro: January is, on average, the UK's coldest month alongside February and one of its wettest and windiest. Most Januaries are dominated by Atlantic westerlies: mild, wet and windy weather with named storms, heavy rain on western hills and only brief cold snaps. But January is also prime time for blocking: a Scandinavian or Greenland high can switch the UK into a cold easterly or northerly regime with snow, ice days and severe frost. Snow is more likely now than in December.

compare.prev: Colder than December on average and more likely to bring lying snow (3.3 days vs 3.0, 1991–2020), with a similar storm risk.
compare.next: Similar to February in temperature; February is usually drier and can be even more prone to late-winter easterlies.

regional: The Highlands and Grampians see the most snow and the coldest glens; föhn can produce exceptional warmth in the lee (19.9 °C at Achfary on 28 January 2024).
Western uplands take the brunt of Atlantic rain; Cumbrian floods (Carlisle 2005) often come in January.
In easterly spells, eastern coasts get North Sea snow showers; in westerlies they are sheltered and often brighter.
Usually mild and damp; lowland snow needs an easterly or a Channel low running into cold air.
months.name: January

months.title: February — late-winter extremes and changing air masses
months.tagline: The most variable winter month: record warmth and the Beast from the East have both happened in February.
months.intro: February varies enormously between years because the large-scale pattern often changes during it. Stormy, jet-driven Februaries (2014, 2020, 2022) bring repeated named storms and floods. Blocked Februaries (1947, 2018, 2021) bring the UK's most severe late-winter cold, as the continent is at its coldest and sudden stratospheric warmings from January can be influencing the circulation. And February has also produced extraordinary warmth: 21.2 °C at Kew on 26 February 2019, the UK's highest winter-month temperature.

compare.prev: Similar in temperature to January but usually drier; snow lies on about as many days (3.4 vs 3.3).
compare.next: Colder and more wintry than March, though March can still bring severe cold and snow.

regional: Most exposed to late-winter easterly outbreaks and North Sea snow (2018, 2021).
Atlantic storms and, occasionally, battleground snow when Atlantic lows meet cold air (Storm Emma, March 2018).
Repeated storms on saturated ground bring river floods (Storm Dennis, February 2020).
Snow cover persists longest; severe minimums in snowy glens (Braemar −23.0 °C, February 2021).
months.name: February

months.title: March — early spring and residual winter
months.tagline: Strong sunshine, cold air aloft: showers, hail, late snow and the first warm days.
months.intro: March sits on the boundary between seasons. The sun is now as strong as in early October, but the sea is near its coldest and Arctic air is still available, so March can deliver both the first 20 °C days (24.5 °C at Kew on 30 March 2021) and severe snow (1947's worst blizzards came in March; late March 2013 was one of the harshest spells of that winter). Atlantic storms continue, though usually less frequently than in mid-winter, and dry, sunny, blocked spells become more common.

compare.prev: Milder and sunnier than February, with fewer frost days; but cold snaps can still be severe.
compare.next: Colder and wetter than April on average; showers become more convective into April.

regional: Snow showers and frosts remain common in the north, especially on hills.
Often the first region to see spring warmth, but also exposed to cold easterlies (March 2013).
Atlantic fronts and showers; hail in cold north-westerlies.
months.name: March

months.title: April — sunshine, showers and rapid transitions
months.tagline: April showers are real: cold air aloft over warming land means big convective clouds.
months.intro: April's reputation for showers comes from the contrast between warming land and air that is still cold aloft. Sunny mornings build into hail and thunder by afternoon, then clear to frosty nights. Northerly plunges can still bring snow to hills and occasionally lower down, while southerly or anticyclonic spells give summer-like afternoons (29.1 °C at St James's Park in April 2018). Blocking highs, most common in spring, can make April very dry; others have been record-breakingly wet (2000, 2012). April storms happen too (Hannah 2019, Noa 2023, Kathleen 2024, Dave 2026).

compare.prev: Warmer and sunnier than March, with fewer frosts but more convective showers.
compare.next: Cooler than May and with a higher frost risk; May brings more warmth and stronger storms.

regional: Biggest diurnal range: frosty dawns, warm afternoons, afternoon showers.
Spring is haar season; easterly breezes keep coasts cool while the west is warm.
April storms have been notable here (Hannah 2019).
months.name: April

months.title: May — increasing warmth and convective potential
months.tagline: The sunniest month in many places — and now capable of genuine heat and thunderstorms.
months.intro: In the 1991–2020 UK averages, May is the sunniest month. Warm high-pressure spells become common, and continental air can now bring real heat: May 2026 set a UK May record of 35.1 °C and the first May tropical night. Thunderstorms become more frequent and stronger as surface heating increases, but frost has not gone — ground frost on clear nights in rural hollows remains plausible. Cool, showery or wet spells (May 2024's record rain in northern England) are still possible.

compare.prev: Warmer and sunnier than April, with fewer frosts and stronger convection.
compare.next: Slightly sunnier than June on UK average but cooler; June brings the first heatwaves more often.

regional: Warmest and most likely to see early heat and plume storms.
Haar and onshore breezes can keep coasts much cooler.
Long days; snow still possible on high summits early in the month.
months.name: May

months.title: June — early summer and thunderstorm scenarios
months.tagline: Long days and rising heat; warm or humid weather alone does not guarantee storms.
months.intro: June brings the longest days and, increasingly, the first heatwaves: June 2026 set a UK June record of 38.0 °C with heatwave conditions somewhere every day from 16 to 30 June. Hot plumes from Iberia can bring thunderstorms, though a strong cap or a settled high can keep skies storm-free despite heat. June can also be cool and wet when the jet stream lies over the UK (June 2007, 2012). Coastal haar and sea breezes keep many coasts much cooler than inland.

compare.prev: Warmer than May with more thunderstorms and the first heatwaves.
compare.next: July is on average warmer, with more frequent heat and storms.

regional: Haar can blanket eastern coasts on otherwise hot days.
Long daylight; summer storms (Hector 2018) and occasional heat.
months.name: June

months.title: July — peak summer heat and severe convection
months.tagline: The warmest month on average and home to the UK's temperature records.
months.intro: July is on average the UK's warmest month, and the national records for England, Wales and Scotland were all set in July 2022 (40.3 °C at Coningsby). Persistent highs can bring drought and wildfires; hot, humid plumes bring the summer's most active thunderstorms — isolated cells, multicell clusters and occasionally organised lines and supercells where wind shear permits. But July can equally be cool and wet (July 2007), and a summer windstorm is possible (Evert 2021).

compare.prev: Warmer than June, with more frequent heatwaves and storms.
compare.next: Similar to August, which is usually a little cooler and often more unsettled late in the month.

regional: Highest temperatures and most heat-health risk (urban heat island in London).
Heat here is rarer: the NI record 31.3 °C was set in July 2021.
months.name: July

months.title: August — late-summer instability and transition
months.tagline: Hot plumes and big storms early; the first Atlantic storms and ex-tropical remnants later.
months.intro: August still brings intense heat (38.5 °C at Faversham in August 2003, six days above 34 °C in August 2020) and some of the year's most extreme thunderstorm rainfall (Boscastle 2004, 239.9 mm at East Wretham in 2020). As the month goes on, the Atlantic jet strengthens: named storms in August are uncommon but not rare (Ellen and Francis 2020, Lilian 2024, Floris 2025), and the remnants of hurricanes start to appear (ex-Bertha 2014).

compare.prev: Similar warmth to July; often more unsettled, with stronger Atlantic influence late on.
compare.next: Warmer and more thundery than September; September brings more settled spells but increasing Atlantic storms.

regional: Atlantic storms and intense convective rain on coasts.
Plume storms and record short-duration rainfall.
months.name: August

months.title: September — late summer and the return of Atlantic systems
months.tagline: Often settled and warm early, increasingly stormy late.
months.intro: September often brings some of the year's most settled weather, and residual heat is possible: September 2023 had seven consecutive days above 30 °C, and 10 September was the hottest day of that year. The jet stream strengthens through the month, so the first named storms of the season (which begins in September) and ex-tropical systems become more likely, and slow-moving systems can bring exceptional rain (late September 2024). Fog and mist return on longer, clearer nights; the first frosts and cold snaps arrive in northern glens and uplands.

compare.prev: Cooler and less thundery than August, but often more settled.
compare.next: Warmer and drier than October on average; October is stormier and wetter.

regional: Late heat is most likely here.
First snow on the highest summits and first frosts in glens are possible.
months.name: September

months.title: October — autumn storms and prolonged rain
months.tagline: The Atlantic returns in earnest — but quiet, warm, foggy Octobers happen too.
months.intro: October is one of the UK's wettest months and the start of the main storm season. Deep Atlantic lows, atmospheric rivers and slow-moving fronts bring flood events (Storm Babet 2023, Scotland's record 2-day rain in 2023, the UK's wettest day on 3 October 2020). Ex-tropical storms can arrive (Ophelia 2017). The Great Storm struck on 16 October 1987. Yet October can also bring warmth (29.9 °C on 1 October 2011), long settled spells, fog and the first widespread frosts. Snow returns to the Scottish mountains.

compare.prev: Wetter, windier and cooler than September.
compare.next: Milder than November, with fewer frosts but similar rain and storm risk.

regional: Orographic and atmospheric-river rain: Cumbria, Wales, western Scotland.
First significant mountain snow; atmospheric-river floods.
Autumn windstorms with trees in full leaf (1987, 2013).
months.name: October

months.title: November — storm tracks, cold snaps and early winter
months.tagline: Wet, windy and darkening — with the first proper taste of winter in some years.
months.intro: November is among the wettest months, with repeated Atlantic lows and some of the UK's worst flood events (Cumbria 2009, South Yorkshire 2019, autumn 2000, Storm Bert 2024). Severe windstorms occur (Arwen 2021 brought damaging northerlies; Ciarán 2023 set England's lowest November pressure). Northerly outbreaks can bring snow to Scottish hills and occasionally lower, while high pressure gives fog, frost and freezing fog on long nights.

compare.prev: Colder than October with more frosts, but similar rainfall and storms.
compare.next: Milder than December on average but often equally wet.

regional: Exposed to rare damaging northerly storms (Arwen 2021).
months.name: November

months.title: December — winter storms and seasonal contrasts
months.tagline: Snow at Christmas is one possible scenario — not the expected one.
months.intro: December brings the longest nights and a peak in Atlantic storms and flooding (December 2015, the UK's wettest calendar month on record, was also its mildest December). Cold spells are possible — December 2010 was exceptionally cold and snowy — but on average snow lies less often in December than in January or February. The Met Office notes widespread snow lying on Christmas Day has happened only four times since 1960 (1981, 1995, 2009, 2010), although snow falling somewhere in the UK on Christmas Day is more common.

compare.prev: Colder than November, with more frost and a little more snow.
compare.next: Milder than January on average, with slightly fewer lying-snow days (3.0 vs 3.3).

regional: Snow most likely; föhn warmth also possible (18.7 °C at Achfary, December 2019).
Mild and wet most years; damaging storms possible (Bella 2020).

special.title: A white Christmas?
special.text: For the Met Office, a single snowflake observed falling on 25 December counts. Since 1960 around half of years have had snow falling at 5% or more of stations; widespread lying snow on Christmas Day (over 40% of stations) has happened only in 1981, 1995, 2009 and 2010.

months.name: December

seasonText.winter: December, January and February: the Atlantic is at its most active, so mild, wet, windy weather dominates most winters, with named storms, flooding on saturated ground and coastal surges. Blocking highs can switch the pattern to frost, fog, freezing fog or cold continental and Arctic outbreaks with snow and ice. Snow lies most often in January and February.
seasonText.spring: March, April and May: rapid transitions. The sun strengthens quickly while the sea is at its coldest and Arctic air is still available, so spring brings sunshine and showers, hail and thunder, late frosts and late snow — alongside the year's first warm spells. Blocking is most common in spring, so very dry, sunny springs (2025) and drought development are possible.
seasonText.summer: June, July and August: heatwaves under high pressure, hot continental plumes and the year's most active thunderstorms, with flash flooding from intense downpours, drought and wildfire risk in dry summers. Equally possible: cool, wet summers when the jet stream sits over or south of the UK, and occasional summer windstorms.
seasonText.autumn: September, October and November: the shift from summer-like weather to the Atlantic storm season. Late warmth and long settled spells are common early on; then deep lows, atmospheric rivers and slow-moving fronts bring windstorms and some of the UK's worst floods. Ex-tropical systems can arrive. Fog, first frosts and early mountain snow return as nights lengthen. A quiet autumn can still contain one severe event.

climate.method: Arithmetic mean of each calendar month over 1991–2020 inclusive; a value is published only if all 30 years are present.

scenarios.name: Zonal Atlantic westerly flow

monthNotes.jan: Peak season: mild, wet and windy; frequent named storms when the jet is strong.
monthNotes.jun: In summer the same pattern means cool, cloudy, showery weather rather than storms.
monthNotes.jul: A "washout" summer pattern when it persists.
monthNotes.oct: The classic autumn return of the Atlantic.

scenarios.summary: The jet stream runs more or less straight from west to east across or near the UK, sending a procession of Atlantic lows and fronts across the country with brief ridges of high pressure between them.
scenarios.frequency: A seasonally common pattern in autumn and winter; it occurs in summer too but usually less persistently.

scenarios.name: Slow-moving, amplified (meandering) jet stream
scenarios.summary: Instead of flowing straight, the jet loops north and south in large waves that move slowly. Weather systems stall, so whatever the UK has — heat, cold, rain or drought — tends to persist.
scenarios.frequency: Plausible in any month; amplified patterns and blocking are noted by the Met Office as most common in spring.

scenarios.name: Jet stream unusually far north

monthNotes.jul: In summer the jet usually lies north of the UK anyway; when it sits well north for weeks, summers like 2018 result.
monthNotes.jan: In winter, a northern jet gives mild, often dry weather in the south while Scotland stays wet and windy.

scenarios.summary: With the jet stream displaced north of the UK, Atlantic lows track towards Iceland and Norway while high pressure covers much of the country — especially the south.
scenarios.frequency: Seasonally common in high summer; plausible in other months.

scenarios.name: Jet stream unusually far south

monthNotes.jun: In summer this means lows tracking across southern Britain: the pattern behind the record wet April–July 2012 and summer 2007.
monthNotes.jan: In winter, lows track to the south and cold air can sit to the north: the battleground for snow.

scenarios.summary: With the jet stream pushed south of the UK, Atlantic lows track across southern Britain or France instead of near Iceland. In summer that means cool, wet weather; in winter it can bring cold air in from the north or east.
scenarios.frequency: Plausible in any month; it is the pattern behind several of the wettest UK summers on record.

scenarios.name: Blocking high pressure

monthNotes.apr: The Met Office notes blocks are most common in spring.
monthNotes.jul: A summer block can mean a long heatwave and drought (1976).
monthNotes.jan: A winter block can mean weeks of cold (1963) or of grey, still gloom, depending on where it sits.

scenarios.summary: A large area of high pressure stays nearly stationary and diverts the usual west-to-east procession of weather systems around it, sometimes for weeks.
scenarios.frequency: Plausible in every month; most common in spring.

scenarios.name: Greenland blocking

monthNotes.dec: December 2010 had strong high-latitude blocking with persistent cold.
monthNotes.jun: In summer a Greenland high pushes the jet south: cool, unsettled weather rather than cold.

scenarios.summary: High pressure over or near Greenland diverts the jet stream south. The UK loses its mild westerlies and draws air from the north instead, with lows passing to the south.
scenarios.frequency: Plausible in winter and spring; uncommon as a cold driver in summer.

scenarios.name: Scandinavian blocking high

monthNotes.feb: The classic driver of severe cold: 1947, 2018 ("Beast from the East") and February 2021.

events.title: Winter of 1947 and the March snowmelt floods
events.summary: High pressure over southern Scandinavia set up a pattern that dominated for weeks. Snow fell somewhere in the UK every day for 55 days. When milder air and Atlantic rain arrived in mid-March, meltwater ran off ground still frozen solid, and rivers across England burst their banks; 70% of houses in Selby were flooded.
observations: Drifts up to seven metres deep in Scotland by 12 March.
Woburn fell to −21 °C on 25 February.
Snow depth of 1.65 m near Ruthin in March 1947 — the deepest recorded in an inhabited area of the UK.

events.title: The Great Smog
events.summary: Under an anticyclone, radiation fog formed beneath an inversion that trapped smoke from countless coal fires and factories. It cleared on 9 December. The Clean Air Acts of 1956 and 1968 followed.
observations: About 4,000 people known to have died as a result.
Each day: 370 tonnes of sulphur dioxide converted into 800 tonnes of sulphuric acid.

events.title: The 1953 North Sea flood
events.summary: A storm in the North Sea drove a surge that coincided with a high spring tide. More than 2,500 people died around the North Sea, including 307 in England and 19 in Scotland. Investment in defences such as the Thames Barrier, and in warning systems, followed.
observations: The greatest storm surge on record in the North Sea (Met Office, Storm Arwen report).
About 160,000 hectares of eastern England flooded.

events.title: Winter of 1962–63
events.summary: A high north-east of the British Isles from 22 December dragged bitterly cold winds across the country for most of the winter — the coldest in England and Wales since 1740. Snow covered much of England every day until early March; even sea water froze in some harbours.
observations: Braemar −22.2 °C on 18 January 1963.
Blizzard of 29–30 December with drifts up to 6 m in Wales and south-west England.

events.title: The Great Storm of 1987
events.summary: A depression that formed over the Bay of Biscay deepened rapidly and crossed southern England overnight. 18 people were killed in England and about 15 million trees were blown down. Forecast models in the final day suggested the worst would stay over the Channel.
observations: Strongest UK gust 100 knots at Shoreham (Sussex).
Gusts of 70 knots or more for three to four consecutive hours in south-east England.
Central pressure 953 mb over the western Channel at midnight.
Analysis suggested such conditions over land in south and south-east England might be expected on average once in 200 years; over the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland, once every 30 to 40 years.

events.title: Burns' Day Storm
events.summary: An intense depression tracked across southern Scotland in daylight, bringing severe gales and storm-force winds to much of England and Wales. Winds affected a much larger area than in October 1987 and struck during the day, so there were more casualties: 47 lives were lost.
observations: Wind speeds comparable to October 1987, and higher over parts of southern England and Wales.
47 deaths.

events.title: August 1990 hot spell
events.summary: A widespread hot spell set a new UK record. Road surfaces melted and a Heathrow runway was affected; hospital admissions rose.
observations: 37.1 °C at Cheltenham on 3 August.

events.title: Freezing rain
events.summary: After cold easterlies under high pressure to the north and east, a low moved north across southern England. Rain fell through a warm layer into sub-zero air at the surface and glazed everything. Birmingham reported a 50% increase in hospital admissions; severe icing disrupted South Wales power supplies.
observations: A classic "warm nose" profile above freezing surface air.

events.title: Easter 1998 floods
events.summary: A stationary band of heavy rain over the Midlands caused floods in which five people died and thousands were evacuated. In many rivers flood levels were higher than the record 1947 flood.
observations: Over 75 mm from Worcestershire towards The Wash.
Over 4,200 homes and businesses flooded in England and Wales.

events.title: The Bracknell storm
events.summary: A localised storm after the wettest April on record. Hailstones up to 1.5 cm fell with mostly cloud-to-cloud lightning and some intense ground strikes.
observations: 65 mm in about an hour at Beaufort Park — the 1961–90 May average is 56 mm.
Estimated by the Met Office as a 1 in 112 year event.

events.title: The wet autumn of 2000
events.summary: The wettest autumn on record for England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the UK (series from 1914). Rivers rose to record levels; 10,000 homes and businesses flooded at 700 locations — the most extensive flooding since the snowmelt floods of March 1947.
observations: Highest autumn value in the England and Wales rainfall series from 1766.

events.title: Cambridge record daily rain
events.summary: A slow-moving front over eastern England.
observations: 90.4 mm in 18 hours at Cambridge Guildhall — the highest 24-hour total at the Cambridge sites since 1900 (Met Office estimate: 140-year return period).

events.title: Tornado reports, 15 October 2002
events.summary: A low moving up from the south-west brought heavy rain to southern and eastern England. A tornado was reported in Torbay in the morning and others in Essex later.
observations: Some stations around The Wash had their normal October rainfall in 6 to 12 hours.

events.title: Strong winds, 27 October 2002
events.summary: Gales and severe gales across the south of the UK as a low moved rapidly across the country to Denmark.
observations: Highest hourly mean 68 knots (78 mph) at the Needles.

events.title: Warm, dry and sunny 2003
events.summary: The warmest year in the UK series at the time; August and September were exceptionally dry in many areas, and November brought double the average in parts of the south-east after a dry summer and autumn.
observations: UK 2003: warmest, third driest and second sunniest year in the series from 1961.

events.title: January warmth at Aboyne
events.summary: Record-equalling January warmth in Aberdeenshire.
observations: 18.3 °C at Aboyne, equalling the then UK January record (Aber, 1958 and 1971).

events.title: August 2003 heatwave
events.summary: The UK record of 37.1 °C (Cheltenham, 1990) was beaten at several stations on 10 August.
observations: 38.5 °C at Brogdale, near Faversham, Kent.

events.title: Summer storm, 7–8 July 2004
events.summary: A depression from Spain and France brought unseasonably high winds and heavy rain, followed by thunderstorms.
observations: Over 100 mm in 18 hours at Wittering — double its July 1961–90 average.

events.title: Boscastle flood
events.summary: Thundery downpours formed bands aligned with the wind, holding heavy rain over north Cornwall for hours. Coastal wind convergence and high ground triggered the storms and the local topography concentrated the flood. Around 75 mm fell in two hours; two rivers burst their banks and about two billion litres of water rushed through the village. Nobody died, thanks largely to a huge helicopter rescue.
observations: About 75 mm in two hours — the normal August total.
Comparable past events listed by the Met Office: Martinstown 1955 (279.4 mm in 24 h), Lynmouth 1952 (229.5 mm in 24 h).

events.title: South-east England dry spell 2004–2006
events.summary: For England SE & Central S: 17 of 21 months had below-average rainfall.
observations: Driest equivalent 21-month period since 1932–34 and third-driest in the series from 1914.

events.title: January 2005 stormy spells
events.summary: Two stormy spells in the first half of the month. Northern England took a battering on the 7th and 8th: lorries overturned and 80,000 customers lost power in north-east England.
observations: Many wind-speed records were set during the month.

events.title: Carlisle floods
events.summary: Prolonged rain over the Lake District and Pennines drained into the River Eden. Three people were killed; it was the worst flood in Carlisle since 1822.
observations: A near-stationary front in a westerly airstream, followed by a very deep depression.

events.title: North York Moors flash flood
events.summary: Thundery downpours spread from north-west England across North Yorkshire; Helmsley was among the places flooded.
observations: Just over 50 mm in 30 minutes at Hawnby.
Return periods over 200 years for 30-minute, 1-hour and 3-hour totals (Flood Estimation Handbook method).

events.title: July 2006: record heat and sunshine
events.summary: Anomalously high pressure over northern Europe and a persistent southerly airstream made July 2006 the warmest calendar month in the Central England Temperature series from 1659.
observations: Road-surface repairs estimated at £3.6m in Oxfordshire alone.

events.title: Summer 2007 floods
events.summary: Record June and July rainfall: heavy rain on 24–25 June over Yorkshire and the Humber and on 19–20 July over the south Midlands brought widespread flooding and transport disruption.
observations: July 2007: over twice the average rainfall over large areas of England and Wales, over four times locally in the south Midlands.
Return period of the high totals estimated at over 200 years (Met Office).

events.title: Strong winds 10–12 March 2008
events.summary: A deep low crossed southern Ireland, Wales and Lincolnshire. Strong winds, low pressure and a high tide combined to bring coastal flooding to parts of the south coast.
observations: 946 hPa west of Ireland at 00 UTC on 10 March.

events.title: October snow in south-east England
events.summary: Record low October temperatures and snow. Reading, Hampstead and Odiham recorded a day of snow — unusual for the climate district in October.
observations: Some stations set new October records for low maximum and minimum temperatures.

events.title: Ottery St Mary hailstorm
events.summary: An unstable occluded front with cold northerly air behind it, fed by a moist southerly flow forced up over Woodbury Common, produced about two hours of hail. The hailstones were small, but hail banks reached 1.2 m deep and blocked drains; about 100 people were evacuated.
observations: 187 mm in 27 hours at King's School; an estimated 160 mm in three hours (return period over 200 years).

events.title: Early February 2009 snowfalls
events.summary: Heavy overnight snow across eastern England. Runways closed at Heathrow and all London buses were stopped.
observations: 29 cm at Mickleham, Surrey; 23 cm at Alice Holt Lodge, Hampshire.

events.title: Lake District floods
events.summary: Exceptionally prolonged heavy rain on ground that had already had close to the whole-month November average. Many Lake District rivers exceeded their previous maximum flows by a wide margin.
observations: Over 400 mm on some high ground in 72 hours.
316 mm in 24 hours at Seathwaite.

events.title: Snow and low temperatures, December 2009 to January 2010
events.summary: The most widespread and prolonged spell of its type since 1981/82: frequent snowfalls with little thaw between them, nights often below −10 °C and below −15 °C in Highland glens.
observations: Depths of 10 to 20 cm widely.

events.title: England and Wales drought 2010–2012
events.summary: A sequence of dry months, especially in spring, autumn and winter. One of the ten most significant one-to-two-year droughts for England and Wales in a century; hosepipe bans for six million people in north-west England in 2010. Ended abruptly by the record rain of April–July 2012.
observations: April 2010 to March 2012: equal-driest two-year period for southern England in records from 1910.

events.title: Cornwall floods
events.summary: A line of intense rain developed with a deep autumn low, flooding St Blazey, St Austell, Mevagissey and Lostwithiel. More than 100 properties flooded and the main line to Penzance closed.
observations: 40 mm or more in two hours in places.

events.title: Snow and low temperatures, December 2010
events.summary: Two spells of severe winter weather. Persistent easterly and north-easterly winds brought bitterly cold air from northern Europe and Siberia; eastern Scotland and north-east England saw the heaviest snow, which then spread so that much of the UK lay under snow by early December.
observations: 50 cm or more on higher ground in eastern Scotland and north-east England.
Below −20 °C on occasion in northern Scotland.
Christmas 2010: snow lying at 83% of stations, the highest ever recorded.

events.title: Warm, dry spring 2011
events.summary: The warmest UK spring in 100 years. Rain repeatedly fell in the north-west and failed to reach the south and east.
observations: Parts of Highland Scotland had over 750 mm; some places in East Anglia and Kent had less than 20 mm.

events.title: Early winter storms, late 2011
events.summary: A powerful jet stream sent a succession of deep depressions across the north. The 8 December storm was the most significant for Scotland since January 2005.
observations: Gusts 60 to 70 knots widely in Scotland; mountain summits well over 100 knots (115 mph).

events.title: Winter storm, 3 January 2012
events.summary: The Central Belt's most severe storm for 13 years (since 26 December 1998), part of a turbulent spell from late November.
observations: Gusts well over 70 knots (81 mph) in southern Scotland.

events.title: Record rainfall, April to July 2012
events.summary: A shift of the jet stream to a much more southerly track than normal sent a succession of lows across the southern half of the UK, abruptly ending the 2010–2012 drought. The far north-west of Scotland stayed much drier than average.
observations: April, June and April–July each the wettest on record in the England & Wales series from 1766.
Summer 2012 the wettest for the UK since 1912.

events.title: Snow and low temperatures, late March 2013
events.summary: A month of easterly and northerly winds from northern Europe and Siberia: cold, overcast days with strong wind chill. The worst came on 22–24 March when fronts brought heavy snow and drifting.
observations: Snow and strong north-easterly winds on southern coasts and the Channel Islands on 10–12 March.

events.title: Hot, dry spell July 2013
events.summary: High pressure gave almost unbroken sunshine in the south and west, while easterlies brought low cloud and fog to North Sea coasts.
observations: Over 28 °C widely every day from 13 to 19 July in southern England, the Midlands and East Anglia.

events.title: Autumn storm, 28 October 2013
events.summary: A fast-moving, vigorous depression. Most damage came from trees still in full leaf. Four people were killed and commuter rail was suspended. Judged within the top ten autumn storms for southern England in 40 years, but not in the same category as 1987.
observations: Highest gust 86 knots (99 mph) at Needles Old Battery.
Gusts 60 to 70 knots (69 to 81 mph) across south-east England.

events.title: Winter storms, December 2013 to February 2014
events.summary: A succession of at least 12 major winter storms from mid-December to mid-February: the stormiest period the UK had experienced for at least 20 years. The 5 December storm drove a major North Sea surge. As rain accumulated, concern shifted from wind to flooding — the Somerset Levels were under water for much of the winter and the Thames flooded through Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Surrey. On 5 February the railway at Dawlish was left suspended when its foundations were washed away.
observations: 5 December 2013 surge: 2 m above predicted high water, coinciding with high tide.
Around 6 major storms from late January to mid-February, 2 to 3 days apart.

events.title: Spanish plume events, July 2014
events.summary: Successive plumes of very warm, humid air from Iberia and France were overrun by cooler air aloft, giving several outbreaks of intense thunderstorms.
observations: 62,277 lightning strikes from 17 to 21 July.
45.8 mm in one hour at Norwich Airport on 20 July.

events.title: Ex-hurricane Bertha
events.summary: The remnants of Bertha brought unseasonably windy and very wet weather. North-east Scotland was worst hit: 200 homes were evacuated in Elgin.
observations: Some places in north-east Scotland had double the August average rainfall.

events.title: One-day heatwave, 1 July 2015
events.summary: Hot air from Spain set a new July record; the heat also triggered thunderstorms in northern England and Scotland.
observations: 36.7 °C at Heathrow.

events.title: Storm Desmond and the Cumbria floods
events.summary: Exceptional rain over the Cumbrian fells fell on ground already saturated by a very wet November, causing widespread flooding — following Carlisle 2005 and Cumbria 2009.
observations: 341.4 mm at Honister Pass in 24 hours to 1800 GMT on 5 December — the UK 24-hour record.
405.0 mm at Thirlmere over two rain-days — the UK 2-day record.

events.title: Wettest calendar month on record, December 2015
events.summary: A persistent, exceptionally mild south-westerly flow of tropical maritime air brought a series of Atlantic lows, including storms Eva and Frank. Boxing Day rain flooded parts of Lancashire, north Manchester and West Yorkshire.
observations: December 2015 was the wettest calendar month for the UK in a series from 1910.
Also easily the mildest December in the UK series from 1910 and the Central England Temperature series from 1659.

events.title: September 2016 heat and storms
events.summary: A southerly flow from France and Spain brought exceptional heat; humidity fed thunderstorms with flash flooding.
observations: 34.4 °C at Gravesend — the highest September temperature since 1911.
Several hourly totals over 30 mm.

events.title: Hot spell June 2017
events.summary: High pressure drew warm air from the near continent; rails were speed-restricted and air pollution rose.
observations: 34.5 °C at Heathrow on 21 June — the highest June temperature since 1976.

events.title: Ex-hurricane Ophelia
events.summary: On the 30th anniversary of the Great Storm, ex-Ophelia brought very strong winds to western Britain and Ireland, where three people died. Thousands of homes in Wales and Northern Ireland lost power.
observations: Gusts of 60 to 70 knots or higher on exposed Irish Sea coasts, especially west Wales.

events.title: 'Beast from the East' and Storm Emma
events.summary: Daytime temperatures stayed widely below freezing with a strong east wind; snow showers organised along convergence lines and the Met Office issued two red warnings for snow — first for the Central Belt, then when Storm Emma pushed mild, moist air north into the cold air over southern England and south Wales. Freezing rain followed in southern areas. The most significant spell of snow and low temperatures for the UK since December 2010.
observations: Two red warnings for snow.
Cars stranded overnight on roads in Scotland and England; Glasgow airport closed.

events.title: Exceptional April warmth, 2018
events.summary: High pressure over the near continent drew very warm air from the south.
observations: 29.1 °C at St James's Park on 19 April — the UK's warmest April day since 1949.
15.9 °C minimum at Kenley — a UK April record.

events.title: Summer 2018
events.summary: High pressure dominated June and July: the warmest UK summer since 2006, the driest since 2003 and the sunniest since 1995.
observations: A run of over 50 dry days at some south-eastern stations, lasting until late July.
30 °C exceeded fairly widely on 15 days.
A Met Office study found a summer this hot is about 30 times more likely now than before the industrial revolution.

events.title: Storm Hector
events.summary: Unseasonably strong winds after weeks of largely fine, settled weather.
observations: A few gusts over 60 knots (69 mph) in Northern Ireland, North Wales and northern England.

events.title: Storms Ali and Bronagh
events.summary: A powerful jet stream drove two storms that marked an emphatic transition from the fine summer of 2018 to autumn. Ali was one of the most notable storms at that time of year in recent decades.
observations: Ali: gusts widely over 60 knots (69 mph) across the north.
Bronagh: well over 50 mm of rain on upland Wales and the south Pennines.

events.title: Storm Callum
events.summary: One of the most significant extreme rainfall and flood events in south Wales in 50 years. The front also produced a temperature contrast of more than 10 °C, with unseasonable warmth in eastern England.
observations: 100 to 150 mm over much of the Brecon Beacons in two days, up to 200 mm on high ground.

events.title: Storm Deirdre
events.summary: Wind, rain and Highland snow — and freezing rain that caused multiple accidents, particularly on the M74 and across southern Scotland. The A66 across the North Pennines closed.
observations: Freezing rain on contact with cold surfaces.

events.title: Winter warmth, February 2019
events.summary: High pressure over the near continent drew an exceptionally mild southerly flow from Iberia and North Africa.
observations: 21.2 °C at Kew Gardens on 26 February — the UK's highest temperature on record for a winter month.

events.title: Storm Hannah
events.summary: For Wales, one of the most significant April storms in 50 years. Trees coming into leaf were brought down.
observations: Gusts over 60 knots (69 mph) in exposed west Wales.

events.title: Wainfleet flood
events.summary: A slow-moving front between cooler air to the north-west and warm, moist air over the near continent gave about 2.5 times the June average in three days. The River Steeping burst its banks and around 600 homes in Wainfleet were evacuated.
observations: About 2.5 times the monthly average rainfall from 10 to 12 June in parts of Lincolnshire.

events.title: July 2019 heatwave
events.summary: A short but exceptional heatwave: a light southerly drew exceptionally hot air from the near continent. Rails buckled and overhead wires sagged in the heat.
observations: 38.7 °C at Cambridge Botanic Garden — the UK record at the time.

events.title: Yorkshire Dales flash floods and Whaley Bridge
events.summary: Thunderstorms caused flash flooding in Swaledale and Arkengarthdale: a bridge collapsed near Grinton. The next day, damage to the spillway of Toddbrook Reservoir led to thousands being evacuated from Whaley Bridge.
observations: 40 to 60 mm in one hour in parts of North Yorkshire; 60 to 80 mm or more in two hours.

events.title: Storm Lorenzo
events.summary: A mid-Atlantic hurricane weakened rapidly as it tracked past the Azores towards Ireland. Limited impacts across the UK.
observations: Mainly affected the west of Ireland.

events.title: Strong winds, 2 November 2019
events.summary: A low brought very strong winds to south Wales and the English south coast. A woman was killed by a falling tree in Dorset.
observations: 95 knots (109 mph) at Needles Old Battery; 72 knots at Plymouth; 71 knots at Culdrose.

events.title: South Yorkshire floods
events.summary: A slow-moving front gave around a whole month's rain in 24 hours on catchments already saturated since late September. The Derwent and Don flooded severely; about 500 homes flooded around Doncaster.
observations: 50 to 100 mm from the Humber to Sheffield in 24 hours.

events.title: December record: föhn in Sutherland
events.summary: A very mild southerly tropical maritime flow crossing the West Highlands warmed by föhn on the lee side, around 02 UTC.
observations: 18.7 °C at Achfary — the UK's highest December temperature on record.

events.title: Storm Ciara
events.summary: The most significant storm for gust speeds across England and Wales overall since 12 February 2014, with persistent heavy rain over the uplands of north-west England. The Humber Bridge closed for only the second time in its history.
observations: Gusts over 60 knots widely across England and Wales.
Over a month's rain in about 18 hours in parts of West Yorkshire.

events.title: Storm Dennis
events.summary: A week after Ciara, Dennis brought 50 to 100 mm or more to western uplands on saturated ground. A red warning for rain covered parts of south Wales; the Wye and Severn were reported at their highest-ever levels and over 1,400 homes and businesses flooded.
observations: Over 600 flood warnings and alerts from the Environment Agency.

events.title: Exceptionally hot day, 31 July 2020
events.summary: A deep low to the west drew hot continental air north for a single day — 30.4 °C the day before and 27.7 °C the day after.
observations: 37.8 °C at Heathrow — then the UK's third-hottest day.

events.title: August 2020 heatwave
events.summary: Hot, humid air from the near continent: one of the most significant heatwaves in southern England in sixty years. Thunderstorms brought hail, lightning fires and flash flooding that closed part of the M25.
observations: Over 34 °C somewhere in the south-east for six consecutive days.
Several tropical nights above 20 °C.

events.title: North-east Scotland thunderstorms
events.summary: A line of severe thunderstorms crossed north-east Scotland while southern England baked at 34 to 35 °C. The torrential rain seems likely to have been a factor in the landslip that derailed a train at Stonehaven, killing three people.
observations: 30 to 50 mm or more within three hours in places.

events.title: Extreme Norfolk rainfall
events.summary: Thunderstorms gave a remarkable daily total at East Wretham. Flood impacts were relatively modest because the extreme rain was very localised, in a rural, low-lying area — a reminder that rainfall amount and flood impact are not the same thing.
observations: 239.9 mm at East Wretham — a new UK August daily record for an individual station.

events.title: Storms Ellen and Francis
events.summary: A strong jet stream drove deep lows across the UK in late August: two of the most notable August storms of the last 50 years. Trees in full leaf on saturated ground came down; beach huts at Woolacombe were washed away.
observations: 69 knots (79 mph) at Capel Curig (Ellen); 70 knots (81 mph) at Needles Old Battery (Francis).

events.title: Storm Alex and the UK's wettest day
events.summary: Alex marked an emphatic transition to unsettled autumn weather; associated fronts brought prolonged, widespread heavy rain on 3–4 October.
observations: UK area-average 31.7 mm on 3 October 2020 — the UK's wettest day on record in a daily series back to 1891.

events.title: Storm Christoph
events.summary: One of the wettest 3-day periods on record for north-west England and North Wales. As the storm cleared it brought significant snow and blizzards over the north-east uplands. Much of Northwich town centre was under water.
observations: 100 mm or more over upland areas.

events.title: Severe winter weather and storm Darcy
events.summary: Easterly winds drew bitterly cold air from eastern Europe. Persistent snow showers built significant accumulations in eastern England and Scotland; Kent and Essex were particularly affected. The most severe wintry spell since the 2018 Beast from the East.
observations: Braemar −23.0 °C — the UK's lowest temperature since December 1995.
20 to 30 cm or more of lying snow in parts of eastern Scotland.

events.title: March warmth then an April plunge, 2021
events.summary: Unusual warmth at the end of March was followed by a cold plunge in early April as a brisk northerly brought Arctic maritime air with wintry showers and widespread hard frosts.
observations: 24.5 °C at Kew on 30 March.
A fall of about 15 °C in a week; several stations had their lowest April temperature for over 40 years.

events.title: Northern Ireland temperature record
events.summary: A week of heat in the west. The Met Office issued the UK's first extreme heat warning. The spell ended in a thundery breakdown with flash flooding in south-east England.
observations: 31.3 °C at Castlederg, County Tyrone, on 21 July — the all-time Northern Ireland record.

events.title: Storm Evert
events.summary: Unusually strong winds for the time of year flattened tents on busy holiday campsites.
observations: 67 knots (77 mph) at Needles Old Battery.

events.title: Heavy and persistent rain, October 2021
events.summary: A slow-moving front produced a 'warm-conveyor' event, very similar to December 2015 and November 2009. About 40 properties flooded, while over 1,200 were protected by defences.
observations: Over 400 mm on the Lake District fells in six days.
Two gauges recorded daily totals over 200 mm on the 27th.

events.title: Storm Arwen
events.summary: A red warning for wind was issued as a developing storm tracked south to the north-east of the UK, bringing damaging NORTHERLY winds. The unusual wind direction may have contributed to the number of trees felled. Three people died and more than a million homes lost power, over 100,000 for several days.
observations: Highest gust 85 knots (98 mph) at Brizlee Wood, Northumberland.
Northerly gusts widely over 60 knots (69 mph).

events.title: Exceptionally mild New Year 2021/22
events.summary: A flow of exceptionally mild tropical maritime air from the Azores, with overcast nights keeping minimums high.
observations: UK's warmest New Year's Eve (16.8 °C, Colwyn Bay) and New Year's Day (16.3 °C, St James's Park).
13.2 °C minimum at Chivenor — a UK January record for highest minimum.

events.title: Storms Malik and Corrie
events.summary: Two storms 36 hours apart brought damaging north-westerly winds. Two people were killed by falling trees.
observations: Corrie: 80 knots (92 mph) at Stornoway Airport; 79 knots at Inverbervie.

events.title: Storms Dudley, Eunice and Franklin
events.summary: Three named storms in a week, the first time since naming began in 2015/16. Eunice brought two rare red warnings and was the most severe and damaging storm to affect England and Wales since February 2014. Four people died in the UK and Ireland from falling trees and over a million homes lost power.
observations: Gust of 106 knots (122 mph) at Needles Old Battery, Isle of Wight — a new England gust record.
Gusts over 60 knots (69 mph) widely across southern England.
Severe coastal flooding in the Severn Estuary avoided: the surge missed high tide by as little as 90 minutes in places.

events.title: 40 °C: the July 2022 heatwave
events.summary: Hot air moved north from the near continent. 40 °C was recorded in the UK for the first time — a milestone in UK climate history — and national records fell in England, Wales and Scotland.
observations: 40.3 °C at Coningsby, Lincolnshire, on 19 July — UK record by 1.6 °C.
Wales 37.1 °C (Hawarden Airport, 18th); Scotland 34.8 °C (Charterhall, 19th).
England's highest daily minimum: 26.8 °C at Shirburn Model Farm on 19 July.

events.title: Prolonged low temperatures, December 2022
events.summary: An Arctic maritime air mass brought hard frosts even in cities and on coasts, with widespread though generally shallow snow. Four children died after falling through the ice on a lake near Solihull.
observations: Braemar −9.3 °C maximum on 12 December — the UK's lowest maximum (excluding mountain sites) since December 2010.
Minimums widely −5 to −10 °C.

events.title: September 2023 heatwave
events.summary: Over 30 °C somewhere in the UK for seven consecutive days — the longest such September run on record. 10 September was, unusually, the hottest day of the year.
observations: 33.5 °C at Faversham, Kent, on 10 September.
Northern Ireland September record 28.0 °C at Castlederg.

events.title: Storm Agnes
events.summary: An intense low enhanced by energy from Tropical Storm Ophelia, weakening before it reached the UK. Impacts were relatively modest overall.
observations: 73 knots (84 mph) at Capel Curig — the equal-highest September gust for Wales.

events.title: Atmospheric river over Scotland
events.summary: A narrow stream of moisture-laden air gave the wettest 2-day period on record for Scotland, while England and Wales reached the low 20s °C on the warm side of the front. Ten people were airlifted from their vehicles when a landslip closed the A83.
observations: 100 to 150 mm widely over the Southern and Central Highlands.
25 °C in parts of south-east England at the same time.

events.title: Storm Babet
events.summary: A blocking high over Scandinavia held the system in place, bringing exceptional rain to eastern Scotland (two red warnings for rain) and heavy, widespread rain across England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
observations: 150 to 200 mm in the wettest parts of eastern Scotland.
For Angus, 19 October 2023 was by a wide margin the wettest day in a series from 1891.
The Midlands provisionally recorded its wettest 3-day period on record.

events.title: Storm Ciarán
events.summary: An exceptionally severe storm for the time of year. Its track meant northern France and the Channel Islands bore the brunt, with winds comparable to south-east England in October 1987; for the UK, recorded winds were fairly typical of a major Atlantic storm. Intense squally rain bands crossed the Channel Islands with very large hail and a reported tornado in Jersey.
observations: 953.6 hPa at Culdrose and St Catherine's Point, which the Met Office reports as England's lowest November pressure.
Gusts of 60 to 70 knots (69 to 81 mph) on the south coast.

events.title: Stalybridge tornado (Storm Gerrit)
events.summary: During Storm Gerrit, a mini-tornado damaged around a hundred homes in Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, and a major incident was declared. The storm also brought heavy Highland snow.
observations: Intense rain over the south Pennines on radar an hour earlier.

events.title: Storms Isha and Jocelyn
events.summary: Two storms in quick succession driven by a powerful jet stream, itself intensified by a large temperature contrast across North America. Isha brought an amber warning over more than half the UK and an overnight red warning for north-east Scotland.
observations: Gust of 86 knots (99 mph) in Northumberland.
Most significant widespread wind storm since Eunice in February 2022.

events.title: January record: föhn in the Highlands
events.summary: A localised föhn effect in north-west Scotland. The Met Office notes that föhn is the main cause of highly localised winter temperature extremes in Scotland and Wales, rather than the milder south of England.
observations: 19.9 °C at Achfary — 13.0 °C above its January average and 1.6 °C above the previous UK January record.

events.title: Storm Kathleen
events.summary: An unusually deep low for the time of year. Kathleen and storm Noa (April 2023) were the most significant April windstorms since April 2013.
observations: Gusts widely over 50 knots on western and northern coasts.

events.title: Exceptionally wet weather, May 2024
events.summary: A slow-moving front around a low off the east coast. A schoolgirl died in a mudslide in North Yorkshire and the West Coast Main Line closed.
observations: 22 May: northern England's wettest spring day in a series from 1891.
75 to 100 mm in the wettest places.

events.title: Wettest month on record for parts of the Midlands
events.summary: A series of lows in a south-easterly flow of unstable air brought thunderstorms and torrential rain; several hundred properties flooded across Hertfordshire, Bedfordshire, Northamptonshire and Oxfordshire.
observations: Oxfordshire and Bedfordshire recorded their wettest calendar month on record (series from 1836).
Oxford recorded its wettest calendar month for 250 years.

events.title: Storm Bert
events.summary: A multi-hazard storm with extremely wet and windy weather; over 150 mm on the wettest uplands of South Wales and south-west England, with gusts over 60 knots even at some inland locations.
observations: 23 November was the UK's wettest day as an area average since 3 October 2020.

events.title: Storm Darragh
events.summary: A red warning for wind covered West Wales and both coasts of the Bristol Channel. Two weeks after storm Bert, a further 50 to 100 mm fell over upland Wales.
observations: Gusts 60 to 70 knots or higher in the red-warning area.
Broadly comparable with Isha, slightly less severe than Eunice; 12 February 2014 was much more severe.

events.title: Rain, wind and Pennine snow, New Year 2024–25
events.summary: Very wet and windy, with significant snow on high ground. Severe flood warnings for the Aviemore and Carrbridge area; several long-running stations in eastern England had their wettest January day on the 5th.
observations: Northern Scotland's third-wettest 3-day period on record (29–31 December).
10 to 20 cm or more of snow across much of the Pennines, with drifting.

events.title: Storm Éowyn
events.summary: The UK's most powerful wind storm for over a decade and, for Northern Ireland, the most significant since the Boxing Day Storm of 1998. A red warning covered all of Northern Ireland and Scotland's Central Belt; the public were advised to stay at home and schools closed.
observations: Highest gust 87 knots (100 mph) at Drumalbin, Lanarkshire.
Tiree recorded the UK's lowest pressure since storm naming began in autumn 2015.

events.title: Spring 2025
events.summary: High pressure building from the Azores or the continent dominated, blocking Atlantic fronts. The UK's warmest, sunniest and sixth-driest spring on record — sunnier than all but three historical summers.
observations: A large positive pressure anomaly between Scotland and Norway, particularly in April.

events.title: Storm Floris
events.summary: One of the most severe summer wind storms to affect Scotland in the observational record. The East Coast Main Line closed north of Newcastle and over 70,000 properties lost power.
observations: Gust of 71 knots (82 mph) at Wick Airport, equalling Scotland's August gust record.

events.title: Storm Amy
events.summary: An unusually severe, though not unprecedented, October storm for Scotland and Northern Ireland, with heavy rain on top of the wind.
observations: Gusts over 80 knots (92 mph) at the most exposed sites.
100 to 150 mm of rain on western and northern uplands in the first four days of October.

events.title: Storm Claudia
events.summary: Parts of England and Wales had the whole-month November average in six days. A major incident was declared in Monmouth as the River Monnow flooded; over 50 properties flooded and 18,000 were protected by defences.
observations: Several severe flood warnings issued.

events.title: Deep snow in northern Scotland
events.summary: A northerly airflow brought persistent snow showers. Aberdeenshire Council declared a major incident and hundreds of schools closed. The Met Office notes depths this great are comparatively unusual, particularly in a warming climate.
observations: 30 to 50 cm in the worst-affected areas, lying for about a week.

events.title: Storm Goretti
events.summary: A multi-hazard storm: damaging winds in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, and widespread lying snow on its northern flank across much of Wales, parts of the West Midlands and the South Pennines. One of the most impactful storms in the far south-west in recent decades.
observations: Gust of 86 knots (99 mph) at St Mary's Airport — the highest on the Isles of Scilly for 47 years.

events.title: Storm Chandra
events.summary: Part of a sequence of lows in late January: the whole-month January average fell widely across south-west England, north-east Scotland and eastern Northern Ireland in eight days. Widespread flooding in Devon, Cornwall and Dorset.
observations: Over 50 mm widely and up to 100 mm on high ground in the worst-affected areas.

events.title: Storm Dave
events.summary: The most severe April windstorm since storm naming began in autumn 2015, judged by the number of stations exceeding 50 and 60 knots. The most severe April windstorm in the observational record remains 1 April 1994.
observations: Gust of 81 knots (93 mph) at Capel Curig — its highest April gust in a 30-year record.
UK April gust record: 87 knots (100 mph) at Flat Holm, 1 April 1994.

events.title: May 2026 late-spring heatwave
events.summary: High pressure and warm continental air brought record-breaking May heat; the Met Office ranks it among the most extreme high-temperature events in the UK record once the time of year is taken into account.
observations: UK May record 35.1 °C at Kew Gardens, beating the old record by over 2 °C.
UK May minimum record 21.4 °C — the first tropical night recorded in May.

events.title: June 2026 humid heatwave
events.summary: Heatwave conditions somewhere in the UK every day from 16 to 30 June as high pressure over Europe moved north. Red heat warnings for three consecutive days in south-east England — the longest run since 2021. The Met Office highlighted extraordinarily high lightning activity.
observations: New UK June record: 38.0 °C at Lingwood, Norfolk, on 26 June.
UK highest June minimum: 23.2 °C at Hastings.
